items.headline: Users abandon onboarding over too many upfront choices
items.background: Onboarding flows have gotten more configurable over the past few years, with many products asking users to set preferences before they've seen any value.
keyFindings: A study of 40 onboarding flows found decision count in the first 30 seconds predicted drop-off better than information volume.
Flows with 3+ upfront choices lost roughly twice as many users as flows with 1 or none.
items.implications: Push non-essential choices past the first screen — defer them until the user has a concrete reason to care.

items.headline: Search is replacing long dropdown menus
items.background: As product catalogs and option lists grow, traditional select-dropdowns are starting to break down as a pattern.
keyFindings: Several major products swapped long dropdowns for a type-to-search field.
Selection time dropped by roughly half in their internal usability tests.
items.implications: If any of your dropdowns exceed ~15 options, a search field will likely outperform them without a full redesign.

items.headline: A 5-minute manual accessibility check you're probably skipping
items.background: Automated accessibility scanners catch a lot, but they systematically miss certain interaction-based issues.
keyFindings: Tabbing through a screen with no mouse reveals focus-order and keyboard-trap issues scanners consistently miss.
Most teams only run this check during formal audits, not before every ship.
items.implications: Add this as a two-minute step before every ship, not just at audit time.

items.headline: Why I stopped using modals for confirmation dialogs
items.background: A designer reflects on a pattern they used for years across multiple products before reconsidering it.
keyFindings: Modals interrupt flow and are frequently dismissed without being read.
Inline confirmation (undo-based patterns) preserved user trust better in their own testing.
items.implications: Consider whether a destructive action truly needs a blocking modal, or whether an undo pattern would serve users better.

items.headline: What 3 years of freelance UX work taught me about scope creep
items.background: A freelancer shares patterns noticed across dozens of client engagements.
keyFindings: Scope creep most often enters through 'quick' verbal requests, not written ones.
Projects with a written change-request process had measurably fewer disputes.
items.implications: Put even small scope changes in writing, regardless of how minor they seem in the moment.
